content.title: Can a struggling Christian have assurance of salvation?
content.summary: Distinguish Christ’s preserving promise, the reality of living faith and the believer’s changing sense of assurance.

answer.text: Yes. The ground of salvation is Christ’s work and promise, not the strength of our feelings. God preserves those truly united to Christ (the site’s confession, the Baptist Faith and Message 2000, says true believers “will never fall away from the state of grace”, article V), yet their assurance can be weakened by sin, temptation or suffering. Scripture directs us to Christ, calls us to examine the fruit of faith and teaches us to seek the Spirit’s help through ordinary Christian life.

reasoning.text: Jesus gives his sheep eternal life and promises that no one will snatch them from his hand. Their safety rests in his power rather than their independence.
Living faith bears fruit, including repentance and love. A bare claim to know Christ while embracing darkness must be tested rather than automatically reassured.
Genuine believers can wait and struggle before attaining settled assurance. Its absence is not itself proof that Christ has rejected them.

conclusion.text: Look to Christ, confess sin and continue in the means he gives: his Word, prayer and the fellowship of the church. Assurance should strengthen grateful obedience and patient hope.

sections.text: Perseverance concerns God’s preservation of his people in faith. Assurance concerns the believer’s knowledge of that grace. Presumption treats a profession, past experience or church connection as permission to ignore Christ. Keeping these distinct protects both the tender conscience and the seriousness of repentance.
sections.title: Perseverance, assurance and presumption

sections.text: The evidence of grace is real but imperfect. A believer’s battle against sin is not the same thing as sinless perfection. Examine yourself in the light of Scripture without turning inward examination into a replacement for Christ’s righteousness. The question is where you are resting and whether you are turning to him in repentance.
sections.title: Fruit without perfectionism

content.objection: Does perseverance mean the warning passages can be ignored?

reply.text: No. Scripture commands Christians to exhort one another and warns against an unbelieving heart. The warnings call us to persevere; they are not permission to assume that every professing believer is secure. The Reformed confessions, Westminster and the Baptist confession of 1689 alike, join God’s preserving grace with real dangers, serious falls and the need for repentance.

limit.text: A short guide cannot pronounce on an individual’s spiritual state. Persistent distress or concealed harm deserves patient care, honest confession and help from trustworthy church leaders. Neither a reassuring phrase nor an intense experience replaces the gospel’s call to faith and repentance.

prompt.text: What is troubling your confidence: Christ’s promise, a particular sin, suffering, or the fear that your faith must feel stronger before he will receive you?
